new_statements.quote: 2° Lorsqu'un mot se trouve dans l'intérieur de la proposition, ou d'un mot composé, ou s'il comporte un suffixe, si l'accent ne porte pas sur sa voyelle finale, cette voyelle disparaît. Ce sont ces mots dont nous séparons la voyelle finale par le signe /. Si, au contraire, l'accent porte sur la voyelle finale, le mot ne subit aucune altération. Ex : gon/o, enfant, petit; bis/i, chien; pusa, beau; gonbis pusa t'ilada, un très beau petit chien. [p. 9-10:] Si l'on considère les mots de la forme kag/a, dans lesquels l'accent porte sur la première voyelle, on remarque que, dans la majorité des cas, la voyelle finale est la même que la voyelle accentuée.
new_statements.translation: 2° When a word is inside a clause, or inside a compound, or carries a suffix, if the accent does not fall on its final vowel, that vowel disappears. These are the words whose final vowel we separate with the sign /. If, on the contrary, the accent falls on the final vowel, the word undergoes no alteration. E.g. gon/o 'child, small'; bis/i 'dog'; pusa 'beautiful'; gonbis pusa t'ilada 'a very beautiful little dog'. [pp. 9-10:] If one considers words of the kag/a type, in which the accent falls on the first vowel, one notices that in most cases the final vowel is the same as the accented vowel.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gaden gives no placement rule. Disyllabic words fall into two lexical classes: those accented on the first vowel (kag/a 'tree', gon/o 'child', bis/i 'dog'), which lose their final vowel when not phrase-final or when suffixed, and those accented on the final vowel (pusa 'beautiful', kaga 'leopard'), which are invariable. Membership is marked word by word with the sign / (p. 8: 'Le signe / placé en avant d'une voyelle, indique que cette voyelle disparaît dès que le mot n'est pas isolé ou en finale. Exemple : kag/a, arbre; kag muta, trois arbres. Quand ce signe est absent, le mot est invariable : kaga, panthère'). Accent is thus contrastive and lexically distributed between initial and final vowel, not fixed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned. p. 8 also notes a diacritic marking 'sur les voyelles initiales de quelques mots, une accentuation spéciale, qui n'est pas une aspiration' (a special accentuation on the initial vowels of some words, not an aspiration).
new_statements.exceptions: Loi 4° notes that isolated/final words generally end in a vowel with exceptions (Kapam! vs Malama), which Gaden attributes to 'une tendance au moindre effort appliquée à des intonations différentes'. He observes that kag/a-type words (first-vowel accent) rarely surface in full because of suffixes and the determiner na, and speculates the final vowel assimilated to the accented one.

new_statements.translation: — The sign / placed before a vowel indicates that this vowel disappears as soon as the word is not isolated or final. Example: kag/a 'tree'; kag muta 'three trees'. When this sign is absent, the word is invariable: kaga 'leopard'; kaga muta 'three leopards'.

sources.quote: [§1.4 Tone, p. vi] Like the Sara and Sara Kaba languages, the tone-bearing phonemes in Bagirmi morphemes can have one of three even tones. High tone is marked with an acute accent, Low tone with a grave accent, and Mid tone with a bar. In addition, there exists a fourth contour tone in Bagirmi, High-Low, which has an important grammatical role in verb conjugations. [§1.6 Final Vowel Dropping, pp. xi-xii] In Bagirmi, a large percentage of multi-syllabic words are candidates for vowel-dropping, a process were the vowel is dropped in non-final position. ... In this work, the lexical entry for words of this type will be listed with a slash before the final vowel (e.g. kòl/ò ‘to cut’, kàr/à ‘toad’). ... A number of phonological factors are involved in determining whether a morpheme is candidate for vowel-dropping.
sources.locator: Grammatical introduction, §1.4 'Tone' (p. vi, with §1.4.1-1.4.5 pp. vii-viii) and §1.6 'Final Vowel Dropping' (pp. xi-xii); open PDF of the 2nd edition (morkegbooks.com)

sources.note: The grammatical introduction describes three level tones plus a grammatical High-Low contour (§1.4) and treats the loss of a word's final vowel in non-final position, which Gaden 1909 used as the mark of accent on the first vowel (his kag/a class, likewise written with a slash here), as a process conditioned by syllable shape and vowel quality with lexical exceptions (§1.6). The words stress and accent do not occur except as names of the tone diacritics. Silent on stress rather than contradicting it: an accent-free account of the same facts, with no statement that Bagirmi lacks stress.

sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog sara1341). Eastern SBB languages keep two-tone systems reflecting *SBB; a large 'western' (*OCC) subgroup innovated a new tone in the high frequencies (a third level); in verbs the change correlates systematically with the modification of one tone verb class, in nouns it shows non-systematic, irregular replacements of original tone patterns, attributed to contact with a new linguistic environment.
